I am struggling with this article. The only take away I am certain of, is that it was not a standard weapon. His arguments against the artwork and his analysis of the weapons usefulness is weak. I would not be surprised with this being a special use weapon against specific target types. The assumption that it was intended as an exclusively bludgeoning weapon when there were other experiments throughout history of disarming or shield removing / circumventing weapons. As he states it could have been an experiment in arms. When did they run the experiment? Perhaps it was run multiple times in history? We see a similar emergent concept in the nunchucks and equivalents in Asian weapons. Perhaps it had a short life where it was implemented then quickly countered in following engagements. Certainly any metal that was not being used would have be reused somewhere else.
